Section 6.1 — The Ethics of the Pulpit: Faithful Exposition and Honest Speech

A pulpit is a position of enormous trust, and like every position of trust it can be abused. We have already learned, in Unit 2, how to handle the Word honestly — reading each text in its context and submitting to what the author actually meant. Here we press that into a matter of ethics, for to twist the Scriptures to say what we want them to say, to make a text serve our agenda rather than God's, is not merely poor exegesis; it is a kind of lying in God's name, and there is scarcely a graver sin a preacher can commit. The man in the pulpit speaks as though he speaks the words of God. If he bends those words to his own purposes, he has made the Almighty the endorser of his private opinions, and the people, trusting him, will never know the difference.

From this flows a whole cluster of pulpit sins to be named and shunned. There is manipulation — the working of the congregation's emotions for effect, the engineered tears, the pressure tactics that bypass the mind and the conscience to extract a response the truth itself did not produce. There is the use of the pulpit as a weapon, the preacher who, too cowardly to confront a man privately, instead aims his sermon at him from the safety of the platform where the target cannot answer. And there is plagiarism, which our age has made easy and common: the preaching of another man's labor as though it were your own. To stand and deliver a sermon you did not study, prayed over by someone else, and let your people believe it came from your own communion with God, is theft and deceit braided together. Use the labors of other men, by all means — no preacher is an island — but use them honestly, and let your preaching be the overflow of your own walk with God and your own wrestling with the text.

Behind all of this stands a conviction I have taught for many years: you do not give a sermon, you preach from the soul. Preaching is not a performance to be admired but a man set on fire by the truth, occupying the space God has given him and speaking what he himself has first been gripped by. The pulpit is not a stage, and the preacher who learns to play it as one — preaching for the applause, the reputation, the effect — has traded a holy calling for a cheap one.

Cross-Reference · Doctrinal PreachingThe convictions behind this section — “occupy the space,” “preach from the soul,” preaching as something you are rather than something you do — are developed in the Doctrinal Preaching course (especially Unit 1, What Is Doctrinal Preaching?).
Section 6.2 — Servant Leadership: Authority, Submission, and Impartiality

The pastor genuinely holds authority in the church; Scripture does not pretend otherwise, and the congregation is called to submit to its faithful leaders. But the manner in which that authority is held is everything, and here our Lord drew the sharpest possible line. "You know that those who are considered rulers over the Gentiles lord it over them... Yet it shall not be so among you" (Mark 10:42–43). Not so among you. The world's pattern of leadership — the strong commanding, the great being served — is precisely the pattern Christ forbids to His undershepherds. Peter echoes it exactly: elders are to lead "not as being lords over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:3). The model is the towel and the basin, the King who knelt to wash the feet of men He could have commanded.

Let me put it in a homely picture. I have a big metal yardstick in my shop. When I am working on a large project I do not reach for a retractable tape or a cloth measure; I lay that yardstick down and I know at once what size a thing is. The trouble is that my yardstick reads in feet and inches. I lived years in Canada and now in Mexico, where everything is measured in meters, but my mind is still stuck in the measure I grew up with. We all carry a measuring stick for success, and most of us inherited the world’s. We say a man has done well if he is clever, or good-looking, or a leader, or makes a great deal of money, or is known. We would not likely brag, “My son has become a wonderful servant.” But God’s ruler is a different ruler altogether. On the night before His death, with His disciples still arguing over which of them was greatest, the Lord of glory rose from supper, wrapped a towel around His waist, took a basin, and washed their feet — the task of the lowest servant in the house. Then He said, "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet" (John 13:14). That is the measure. The world asks, “How many people work for you?” The Lord asks, “For how many people do you work?” A man called to lead in Christ’s church is called first to kneel in it.

So the pastor's authority is real but inverted from the world's: it is the authority of a servant, exercised for the good of those served and never for the comfort or aggrandizement of the one who holds it. And the submission Scripture asks of the congregation is the glad following of a shepherd who plainly loves them and points them to Christ — not the cowed obedience extracted by a domineering man who has confused his own will with the will of God. A leader who must demand submission has usually already forfeited the right to it.

One more mark belongs to godly leadership: impartiality. The church is the one place on earth where the distinctions the world lives by are to mean nothing. "My brethren, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with partiality" (James 2:1). The pastor who fawns over the wealthy donor and overlooks the poor widow, who bends the rules for his friends and applies them strictly to those he dislikes, has betrayed the gospel of a God who shows no favoritism. Justice in the church must be blind to wealth, to status, to friendship, and to the leader's own preferences. The same standard, the same patience, and the same grace must reach the influential man and the inconvenient one alike.
Section 6.3 — Biblical Church Discipline — and Its Misuse

Few subjects are more neglected, and few more easily mishandled, than the discipline of the church. Our Lord laid out the process Himself with great care. "If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone" (Matthew 18:15). That is the first step and the one most often skipped: a private word, between the two, aimed at winning the brother. If he will not hear, the second step is to take one or two others, that every word may be established by witnesses. If he still refuses, the matter comes before the church. And only if he will not hear even the church is he finally to be treated as one outside it. Note the patient escalation, each stage giving room for repentance, each stage widening the circle only as far as the brother's hardness requires and no farther.

Alongside Matthew 18 stands the graver case of 1 Corinthians 5, where a notorious, unrepented, public sin in the church demanded decisive action for the sake of the whole body. From these passages we draw the three purposes of all discipline, and they must be held in this order: first, the restoration of the sinning brother, which is always the goal; second, the purity of the church, that a little leaven not corrupt the whole lump; and third, the honor of Christ's name before a watching world. A useful distinction governs the process: private sins are dealt with privately and need never become public if repentance comes early, while sins that are public or that harden into open defiance may require the wider steps.

Now I must speak plainly about something the manuals too often leave unsaid, because nothing in pastoral ministry is more easily turned into a weapon than discipline. The same process our Lord gave for healing can be perverted into an instrument of control, and a great deal of spiritual abuse has been committed under its banner. Discipline is misused when a leader skips the patient private steps and escalates straight to public exposure, satisfying his anger rather than seeking the brother. It is misused when its true engine is the leader's wounded pride and not the sinner's good. It is misused when it becomes a tool for silencing those who question the leadership, or for crushing rather than restoring. Hear me on this: a discipline that has lost the goal of restoration has ceased to be biblical discipline and has become something else, something cruel. Paul fixes the spirit forever: "if a man is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). Restore — not destroy. In gentleness — not in fury. And considering yourself — for the man who corrects another while forgetting his own capacity for the very same sin is the likeliest of all to become a tyrant in God's name. Discipline must always sharpen the leader's own self-examination at least as much as it confronts the offender.
Section 6.4 — The Tongue: Gossip, Destructive Speech, and a Vital Distinction

If the pulpit can be abused and authority can be abused, so above all can the simple human tongue, and Scripture treats it with a seriousness we rarely match. James calls it a fire, "a world of iniquity" set among our members (James 3:6). Solomon warns that "a whisperer separates the best of friends" (Proverbs 16:28). And Paul, listing the sins he feared to find festering in a church, names alongside the grosser vices the quieter killers: "backbitings, whisperings" (2 Corinthians 12:20). We are slow to see gossip as the church-destroyer it is, precisely because it feels so small, so natural, so easily disguised as concern or prayer request. But it is among the chief solvents of Christian unity, and a congregation given to it will be eaten hollow from within while everyone professes love.

The pastor bears a double responsibility here. He must refuse to traffic in it himself — never repeating what he need not repeat, never being the source or the eager hearer of a tale — and he must have the courage to confront it in the flock, gently stopping the whisper at his own door and teaching his people to do the same. A man cannot lead a pure-tongued church while indulging an impure tongue in private.

And now the distinction this unit has been building toward, because it is the one most often abused in both directions. What separates sinful gossip from the legitimate confrontation of sin? Not the subject matter, for both may concern another person's fault. The difference lies in direction, motive, and goal. Gossip talks about a person to those who are neither part of the problem nor part of the solution; biblical confrontation goes to the person, through the very channels our Lord laid out in Matthew 18. Gossip aims to wound, to vent, or to elevate the teller by lowering the subject; discipline aims at the offender's restoration. To carry a brother's sin privately to him, or through the proper steps to those charged with helping, is not gossip — it is obedience. To carry that same sin sideways, into idle conversation with those who can do nothing but think less of him, is gossip however piously it is framed. Learn to tell the two apart, and teach your people to, and you will have done much to guard both the holiness and the unity of the church at once.

Cross-Reference · This CourseThe confidentiality this section assumes was treated in Unit 5; the full process of restoring a disciplined member — evaluating repentance, the 2 Corinthians 2 model, reintegration — is developed in Unit 10.

sa.prompt: 21. Name the pulpit sins the unit warns against and the conviction behind them.
sa.model: To twist the Scriptures to serve our agenda rather than God's is a kind of lying in God's name, for the preacher speaks as though he speaks the words of God. The unit names a cluster of pulpit sins: manipulation that works the emotions to bypass the mind and conscience; using the pulpit as a weapon to attack a man who cannot answer; and plagiarism, preaching another man's labor as though it were your own. Other men's labors may be used, but honestly, as the overflow of one's own walk with God.

es_reference.prompt: 21. Nombre los pecados del púlpito contra los que advierte la unidad y la convicción tras ellos.
es_reference.model: Torcer las Escrituras para servir a nuestra agenda en vez de a la de Dios es una especie de mentira en el nombre de Dios, pues el predicador habla como si hablara las palabras de Dios. La unidad nombra un racimo de pecados del púlpito: la manipulación que trabaja las emociones para esquivar la mente y la conciencia; el uso del púlpito como arma para atacar a un hombre que no puede responder; y el plagio, predicar el trabajo de otro hombre como si fuera el suyo propio. Las labores de otros pueden usarse, pero honestamente, como el desbordamiento del propio andar con Dios.

sa.prompt: 22. Explain 'you do not give a sermon, you preach from the soul.'
sa.model: Preaching is not a performance to be admired but a man set on fire by the truth, occupying the space God has given him and speaking what he himself has first been gripped by. You do not give a sermon; you preach from the soul. The pulpit is not a stage, and the preacher who plays it for applause, reputation, or effect has traded a holy calling for a cheap one.

es_reference.prompt: 22. Explique «usted no da un sermón, predica desde el alma».
es_reference.model: La predicación no es una actuación para ser admirada sino un hombre encendido por la verdad, ocupando el espacio que Dios le ha dado y hablando lo que él mismo ha sido primero asido. Usted no da un sermón; predica desde el alma. El púlpito no es un escenario, y el predicador que lo toca por el aplauso, la reputación o el efecto ha cambiado un llamamiento santo por uno barato.

sa.prompt: 23. How does the unit define servant leadership, drawing on Mark 10 and the towel and basin?
sa.model: Jesus drew the sharpest line: the Gentiles lord authority over others, 'yet it shall not be so among you' (Mark 10:42-43), and Peter echoes it, leading not as lords but as examples (1 Peter 5:3). The model is the towel and the basin, the King who knelt to wash the feet of men He could have commanded. The pastor's authority is real but inverted from the world's: it is the authority of a servant, exercised for the good of those served. The world asks how many work for you; the Lord asks for how many you work.

es_reference.prompt: 23. ¿Cómo define la unidad el liderazgo de siervo, apoyándose en Marcos 10 y la toalla y la palangana?
es_reference.model: Jesús trazó la línea más aguda: los gentiles señorean autoridad sobre otros, «mas no será así entre vosotros» (Marcos 10:42-43), y Pedro lo repite, dirigiendo no como señores sino como ejemplos (1 Pedro 5:3). El modelo es la toalla y la palangana, el Rey que se arrodilló para lavar los pies de hombres a quienes pudo haber mandado. La autoridad del pastor es real pero invertida de la del mundo: es la autoridad de un siervo, ejercida para el bien de aquellos a quienes sirve. El mundo pregunta cuántos trabajan para ti; el Señor pregunta para cuántos trabajas tú.

sa.prompt: 24. What does impartiality require of a leader, and what does James 2:1 forbid?
sa.model: James 2:1 forbids holding the faith of Christ with partiality. The pastor who fawns over the wealthy donor and overlooks the poor widow, who bends the rules for friends and applies them strictly to those he dislikes, has betrayed the gospel of a God who shows no favoritism. Justice in the church must be blind to wealth, status, friendship, and the leader's own preferences. The same standard, patience, and grace must reach the influential and the inconvenient alike.

es_reference.prompt: 24. ¿Qué exige la imparcialidad de un líder, y qué prohíbe Santiago 2:1?
es_reference.model: Santiago 2:1 prohíbe sostener la fe de Cristo con acepción de personas. El pastor que adula al donante rico y pasa por alto a la viuda pobre, que dobla las reglas para sus amigos y las aplica con rigor a los que le disgustan, ha traicionado el evangelio de un Dios que no hace acepción de personas. La justicia en la iglesia debe ser ciega a la riqueza, el estatus, la amistad, y las preferencias propias del líder. La misma norma, paciencia y gracia deben alcanzar al influyente y al inconveniente por igual.

sa.prompt: 25. Lay out the steps of Matthew 18 and the wisdom of its patient escalation.
sa.model: The Lord gave a precise, escalating process. First, a private word between the two alone, aimed at winning the brother—the step most often skipped. If he will not hear, take one or two others as witnesses. If he still refuses, bring it to the church; and only if he refuses even the church is he treated as one outside it. Each stage gives room for repentance and widens the circle only as far as the brother's hardness requires, no farther.

es_reference.prompt: 25. Exponga los pasos de Mateo 18 y la sabiduría de su paciente escalada.
es_reference.model: El Señor dio un proceso preciso y escalonado. Primero, una palabra privada entre los dos a solas, dirigida a ganar al hermano — el paso más a menudo omitido. Si no quiere oír, tome a uno o dos más como testigos. Si aún rehúsa, llévelo a la iglesia; y solo si rehúsa aun a la iglesia es tratado como uno fuera de ella. Cada etapa da lugar al arrepentimiento y amplía el círculo solo hasta donde la dureza del hermano lo requiere, no más.

sa.prompt: 26. State the three purposes of church discipline in their proper order.
sa.model: From Matthew 18 and 1 Corinthians 5 the unit draws three purposes, to be held in this order: first, the restoration of the sinning brother, which is always the goal; second, the purity of the church, that a little leaven not corrupt the whole lump; and third, the honor of Christ's name before a watching world. A useful distinction governs the process: private sins are dealt with privately, while public or defiant sins may require the wider steps.

es_reference.prompt: 26. Exponga los tres propósitos de la disciplina de la iglesia en su orden propio.
es_reference.model: De Mateo 18 y 1 Corintios 5 la unidad saca tres propósitos, que han de sostenerse en este orden: primero, la restauración del hermano que peca, que es siempre la meta; segundo, la pureza de la iglesia, para que un poco de levadura no corrompa toda la masa; y tercero, la honra del nombre de Cristo ante un mundo que observa. Una distinción útil rige el proceso: los pecados privados se tratan en privado, mientras que los públicos o desafiantes pueden requerir los pasos más amplios.

sa.prompt: 27. How is church discipline misused, and what spirit does Galatians 6:1 require?
sa.model: Nothing in ministry is more easily turned into a weapon than discipline. It is misused when a leader skips the patient private steps and escalates straight to public exposure, when its engine is wounded pride rather than the sinner's good, or when it silences those who question leadership. A discipline that has lost the goal of restoration has ceased to be biblical discipline. Galatians 6:1 fixes the spirit forever: restore such a one in gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted.

es_reference.prompt: 27. ¿Cómo se mal usa la disciplina de la iglesia, y qué espíritu exige Gálatas 6:1?
es_reference.model: Nada en el ministerio se convierte más fácilmente en un arma que la disciplina. Se mal usa cuando un líder omite los pacientes pasos privados y escala directo a la exposición pública, cuando su motor es el orgullo herido en vez del bien del pecador, o cuando silencia a los que cuestionan el liderazgo. Una disciplina que ha perdido la meta de la restauración ha dejado de ser disciplina bíblica. Gálatas 6:1 fija el espíritu para siempre: restaurad al tal con mansedumbre, considerándote a ti mismo, no sea que tú también seas tentado.

sa.prompt: 28. Why does the unit treat gossip as a serious church-destroyer?
sa.model: Scripture treats the tongue with a seriousness we rarely match: James calls it a fire, a world of iniquity, and Proverbs warns that a whisperer separates the best of friends. Gossip is among the chief solvents of Christian unity, and a congregation given to it will be eaten hollow from within while everyone professes love. It goes unrecognized precisely because it feels so small and is easily disguised as concern or a prayer request.

es_reference.prompt: 28. ¿Por qué trata la unidad el chisme como un grave destructor de la iglesia?
es_reference.model: La Escritura trata la lengua con una seriedad que rara vez igualamos: Santiago la llama un fuego, un mundo de maldad, y Proverbios advierte que el chismoso aparta los mejores amigos. El chisme está entre los principales disolventes de la unidad cristiana, y una congregación entregada a él será comida por dentro hasta quedar hueca mientras todos profesan amor. Pasa desapercibido precisamente porque se siente tan pequeño y se disfraza fácilmente de preocupación o petición de oración.

sa.prompt: 29. What is the pastor's double responsibility regarding the tongue?
sa.model: The pastor bears a double responsibility. He must refuse to traffic in gossip himself—never repeating what he need not repeat, never being the source or the eager hearer of a tale. And he must have the courage to confront it in the flock, gently stopping the whisper at his own door and teaching his people to do the same. A man cannot lead a pure-tongued church while indulging an impure tongue in private.

es_reference.prompt: 29. ¿Cuál es la doble responsabilidad del pastor respecto a la lengua?
es_reference.model: El pastor lleva una doble responsabilidad. Debe rehusar traficar con el chisme él mismo — nunca repitiendo lo que no necesita repetir, nunca siendo la fuente o el oidor ansioso de un cuento. Y debe tener el valor de confrontarlo en la grey, deteniendo con suavidad el susurro en su propia puerta y enseñando a su gente a hacer lo mismo. Un hombre no puede dirigir una iglesia de lengua pura mientras consiente una lengua impura en privado.

sa.prompt: 30. Explain the vital distinction between sinful gossip and legitimate confrontation of sin.
sa.model: The difference is not the subject matter, for both may concern another's fault; it lies in direction, motive, and goal. Gossip talks about a person to those who are neither part of the problem nor the solution; biblical confrontation goes to the person, through the channels of Matthew 18. Gossip aims to wound or to elevate the teller; discipline aims at the offender's restoration. To carry a sin to the person, or through the proper steps, is obedience; to carry it sideways into idle conversation is gossip, however piously framed.

es_reference.prompt: 30. Explique la distinción vital entre el chisme pecaminoso y la confrontación legítima del pecado.
es_reference.model: La diferencia no es el tema, pues ambos pueden tratar de la falta de otro; yace en la dirección, el motivo y la meta. El chisme habla acerca de una persona a quienes no son ni parte del problema ni de la solución; la confrontación bíblica va a la persona, por los canales de Mateo 18. El chisme busca herir o elevar al que habla; la disciplina busca la restauración del ofensor. Llevar el pecado a la persona, o por los pasos debidos, es obediencia; llevarlo de lado a la conversación ociosa es chisme, por piadosamente que se enmarque.
